of priorities whose office cannot be read, after the repair

points: The route into Australia is filled for 93.69% of rights: every right but provisional applications and plant breeder's rights, which claim nothing.
65.8% of rights claim no priority; the most claimed priority office is the United States (44.6% of rights with one).
8 link dates are placeholders (1800, 1900) and are not used to order priorities.

questions.how: Where an invention was first filed says where it came from, which matters for where its value is created.
Without the repair, every international application would look Australian.

prep.what: An Australian application number (ten digits, year first) is Australian; a PCT number names its receiving office; any other number labelled Australian has an unknown office.
prep.why: The register's country label is wrong for most international numbers (ADR 0022).

steps: Count the register's links by type and how often each is labelled Australian.
Check each labelled number against the pattern of an Australian number.
Read each patent priority's office from its number, and count those left unreadable.
assumptions: A number's format reliably shows the office that issued it.
limits: Trade mark and design priorities keep the register's label, which is sound for them.

Take WIPO's counts for the same office and years.
Divide one by the other, year by year, and summarise the ratios.
assumptions: WIPO's counts, which IP Australia reports to it, are an independent benchmark.
limits: Agreement in totals does not prove every individual link is right.

observations.headline: Overseas applicants come through the international route; Australians have moved from provisionals to the PCT, divisionals and direct filing
observations.statement: The international (PCT) route carried 81.0% of overseas applicants' standard patents in FY2010 and 69.3% in FY2026, while divisionals rose to 19.9%. Australians claiming only an Australian application (usually a provisional) fell from 81.2% (FY1985) to 11.4% (FY2026), and direct filing, claiming nothing, reached 28.3% in FY2026.

figures.label: of overseas standard patents came through the PCT in FY2010
of Australians' standard patents filed directly in FY2026, a lead

points: Australians' use of the PCT rose from 7.8% to 45.2% (FY2020) and 34.6% (FY2026); divisionals from 2.0% to 22.2%.
Trade marks: Australians' are 97.9% to 99.1% direct; from overseas, the Madrid system carried 36.7% in FY2005, 57.2% in FY2020 and 44.0% in FY2026.
Designs from overseas claim a priority abroad for 70.7% (FY1985) to 87.5% (FY2010) and 75.8% (FY2026).
The rise in direct filing is a lead: a change in practice, or priority claims recorded late.

questions.how: How inventions reach Australia shows how the system connects to others, and where Australian inventions start.
Routes into other markets (PCT, Madrid) are part of how Q3's "access to international markets" works.

prep.what: Each right's route is the first that applies, in the order PCT, divisional, priority abroad, Australian priority, direct (Madrid for trade marks).
prep.why: A right can claim several things; one route each keeps the shares adding to 100%.

steps: Give each right its route.
Count rights by type, origin, filing year and route.
Work out each route's share of each year's applications.
assumptions: The order of routes reflects how the application actually entered Australia.
limits: Recent direct filings may still have priority claims added; the FY2026 figure may change.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares routes by origin, applicant and technology.

observations.headline: Google Patents finds the worldwide family of nearly every standard patent filed since the 1980s
observations.statement: The family is found for 98.78% of standard patents filed in the 1980s, 98.99% (1990s), 94.81% (2000s), 99.23% (2010s) and 98.14% (2020s). Provisional applications, which are rarely published, are almost never found.

questions.how: How widely an invention is protected is a widely used sign of its expected private value.
Australians, and individuals most, protect more narrowly, which bears on who gets value from inventing.

prep.what: Standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019 are used.
prep.why: They are nearly all decided, and five years of citations are complete for most.

steps: For each standard patent, take the number of offices its family reached and whether the US granted it.
Summarise by the applicant's origin, and for Australians by individual or organisation.
assumptions: Filing in more offices reflects higher expected value, as the literature commonly assumes.
limits: Reach also depends on markets and budgets; a small firm may value a patent it can afford to file only here.

points: The spread is a long tail: the 99th percentile is 136 citing families for overseas applicants' patents and 44 for Australians'.

prep.what: Citations are counted as distinct later families citing the family within five years of its first filing.
prep.why: A fixed window treats old and new patents alike; the count is empty where the window is not complete.

steps: For standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, take each family's five-year citation count.
Summarise by origin (median, share never cited, 99th percentile).
assumptions: A citation means the later invention builds on, or is close to, the cited one.
limits: Citations reflect family size, field and examiners' practice, not only importance.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares citations as ranks or logs, within cohorts and fields, beside family size.

observations.headline: Inventors' countries are missing for most patents filed only in Australia
observations.statement: An inventor's country is known for 87.57% to 97.06% of overseas filers' standard patents each decade, but for only 11.71% (1990s), 22.3% (2000s), 56.98% (2010s) and 64.27% (2020s) of Australian filers'. Of Australian filers' patents with inventors but no country, 94.33% to 99.18% were filed only in Australia, where Google's records give no inventor countries.

inventors named on the median standard patent

points: Inventors are named for 25.7% of rights (patents with a family that names them); standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026 name a median 3 (22.46% name one).
**So** "invented in Australia" describes Australian filers' patents that were also filed abroad, and leaves out most of those filed only here.

questions.how: Limits what can be said about who invents in Australia, and for which patents.

prep.what: Inventors come from one publication per family, the one naming the most, with countries borrowed from the rest of the family.
prep.why: Counting every publication's names nearly doubled the inventors (ADR 0008).

steps: For each patent, count its inventors and those with a known country.
Work out the share with a known country, by type, origin and decade.
For those with inventors but no country, check how many were filed only in Australia.
assumptions: An inventor's recorded country is where they lived when the invention was made.
limits: Patents filed only in Australia, half of Australians', mostly cannot be placed.

observations.headline: Gender estimated from names matches WIPO's figure for Australia, but not for most other countries
observations.statement: For inventors of international applications, the share estimated to be women is 14.6% for Australia, against WIPO's published 13.8%. But the median country is 4.5 points too high, and China (34.6% against 23.4%) and Korea (37.0% against 15.7%) far too high. So estimates are read for inventors in Australia only.

figures.label: Australia, estimated against WIPO's share of women inventors
Korea's estimate above WIPO's

points: The Netherlands, Spain, New Zealand, Finland and Ireland are within 2 points.
The United States 20.0% against 15.3%; Germany 16.6% against 10.7%; Japan 16.3% against 9.0%.
For China, 49.1% of names are between 10% and 90% likely to be a woman's; in Korea only 53.3% of inventors get an estimate.
**Decision.** Estimates are read as levels for inventors in Australia only; for other countries only within one country over time; for China and Korea not at all.

questions.how: Q2 asks how outcomes vary by gender where reliable data exist; this check is what makes the Australian figure usable.

prep.what: Each inventor's chance of being a woman comes from WIPO's World Gender-Name Dictionary, by first name and country.
prep.why: Gender is not recorded anywhere; a name-based probability is the only route, and must be checked.

prep.what: WIPO's share of women among PCT inventors by country was added to the corpus for the check.
prep.why: An independent benchmark is needed before using any estimate (ADR 0022).

steps: For inventors of PCT families first filed 2015 to 2022, average their probabilities by country.
Compare with WIPO's published share for 2016 to 2023, country by country.
For Australia, compare year by year.
assumptions: Summed over many inventors, name-based probabilities give a fair count of women, where names are informative.
limits: An estimate says nothing about any individual.
Recent Australian estimates run above WIPO's (17.2% against 14.4% in 2023).

observations.headline: The firms table holds the businesses that used one of five schemes, not every business, and its IP counts are lower bounds
observations.statement: The table has 398,450 [[abn|ABNs]]. 63.68% appear only because they filed IP in IP RAPID, 13.69% only because they hold a government contract, and 12.75% only because an older IP Australia dataset ([[iplord|IPLORD]]) links them to IP. Anything measured across this table describes these firms, not Australian businesses in general.

figures.label: businesses (ABNs) in the firms table
linked to IP only by IPLORD, so their IP counts read zero
of those IPLORD-only businesses still have an active ABN

points: **Who is in it.** 253,719 ABNs are in IP RAPID alone, 54,552 in AusTender alone, 50,790 linked to IP by IPLORD alone, 8,033 in the R&D Tax Incentive alone and 3,139 in the tax transparency reports alone; the rest appear in two or more.

**Many have closed.** Active ABNs run from 47.02% of the IPLORD-only firms and 59.62% of the firms only in IP RAPID, to 92.02% of R&D claimants and 95.35% of firms in both IP RAPID and the R&D Tax Incentive.
**Filer and holder.** Where both are known, the business that filed a right is not the one that holds it now for 2.17% of standard patents, 7.11% of trade marks and 5.25% of designs.

**IPLORD's own counts are not used.** For the 152,683 ABNs with trade marks in both datasets, 81.02% have the same count, but IPLORD's total is 1.84 times IP RAPID's and its weighted total 0.42 times. They are built differently.
**Gaps.** 63 ABNs are not in the business register extract and 3,875 have no state.

questions.how: Any comparison of who uses the IP system (Q2) must say it is among firms that used a scheme, and that their IP counts are a floor, not the full picture.
The table joins IP to R&D claims, contracts and company records for the same business, which is what Q3 needs to ask what goes with IP producing value.

prep.what: One row per ABN, taken from the corpus's ABN spine, which lists every ABN found in IP RAPID, IPLORD, the R&D Tax Incentive, AusTender or the tax transparency reports.
prep.why: The ABN is the one identifier that links a business across these sources and to the business register.

prep.what: Each application is credited to the business that filed it (its first founding applicant with an ABN), not the business that holds it today.
prep.why: "Who files" should not change when a right is later sold (ADR 0016).

prep.what: A flag marks the ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP; IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
prep.why: IPLORD counts applications differently from IP RAPID, so adding the two would mix two measures.

steps: Count the ABNs in the table, and for each, the sources it appears in.
Group the ABNs by that combination of sources and count each group.
For each group, work out the share whose ABN is still active in the business register.
For rights where both the filer's and the holder's ABN are known, count how often they differ.
Compare IPLORD's trade mark counts with IP RAPID's for the ABNs that appear in both.
assumptions: An ABN stands for one business. Related companies in the same group have different ABNs and are counted separately.
A right with no ABN recorded for its filer cannot be credited to any firm; such rights are left out of firms' counts rather than guessed.
limits: The table is not a census of Australian businesses. A business that never used one of the five schemes is not in it, so rates worked out on this table are rates among scheme users.
Firms' IP counts are lower bounds, because rights with no ABN (and IPLORD-only links) add nothing to them.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares firms' IP with their R&D, contracts, age and type, always stating that the comparison is among scheme users and that IP counts are a floor.

observations.original:
**U41 (descriptive). The lens is the firms that used one of five schemes, not all businesses, and its IP counts are
lower bounds.**
- **Who is in it:** 398,450 ABNs. 253,719 (63.68%) are in IP RAPID alone, 54,552 (13.69%) in AusTender alone, 50,790
  (12.75%) linked to IP by IPLORD alone, 8,033 (2.02%) in the R&D Tax Incentive alone and 3,139 (0.79%) in the tax
  transparency reports alone; the rest are in two or more. Rates computed on the lens are rates among these firms.
- **Active ABNs** run from 47.02% of the IPLORD-only firms and 59.62% of the IP RAPID-only firms to 92.02% of the R&D
  claimants and 95.35% of firms in both IP RAPID and the R&D Tax Incentive: many firms that once filed for IP have
  since closed.
- **Filer against holder:** where both ABNs are known, they differ for 2.17% of standard patents, 7.11% of trade marks
  and 5.25% of designs; 6.04% to 7.25% of rights with a holder's ABN have no filer's ABN.

  built differently.

observations.headline: Private companies make up most firms in every scheme except government contracting
observations.statement: Private companies are 74.7% of all firms in the table, 82.2% of IP filers and 94.5% of R&D Tax Incentive claimants, but only 55.3% of government suppliers, where sole traders (16.2%) and trusts (12.9%) are common.

figures.label: of all firms are private companies
of R&D Tax Incentive claimants are private companies
of government suppliers are private companies

points: The R&D Tax Incentive is open to companies only, so it has no trusts, partnerships or sole traders. That is its rule, not a choice those businesses made.
**Status.** 62.4% of private companies' ABNs are still active, 71.8% of public companies' and 34.3% of partnerships'.
Of active ABNs, 79.5% of private companies and 55.1% of sole traders are registered for GST (roughly, a turnover of $75,000 or more).

questions.how: Shows which kinds of business reach each scheme, the starting point for asking who the IP system serves.

prep.what: Each ABN's entity type from the business register is grouped into eight broad groups (private company, trust, sole trader and so on).
prep.why: The register has 57 entity types; eight groups are enough to compare schemes and few enough to read.

prep.what: An "IP filer" is a firm credited with at least one IP application as a founding applicant.
prep.why: Holding a right bought from someone else is not the same as filing for one.

steps: Group every firm by its entity group.
Within all firms, IP filers, R&D claimants and government suppliers in turn, work out each group's share.
For each entity group, work out the share of ABNs that are active, and of active ones, the share registered for GST.
assumptions: The business register's entity type is taken as recorded; a business that changed form keeps its current type.
limits: Shares describe the firms that used each scheme; they do not say which kinds of business would benefit from using it.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares firms within the same entity group, so that differences between schemes are not mistaken for differences between kinds of business.

**U42 (descriptive). Private companies dominate every source but AusTender.** Of each group's ABNs:
- **Private companies** are 74.7% of all firms, 82.2% of IP filers, 94.5% of R&D claimants and 55.3% of government
  suppliers. The R&D Tax Incentive is open to companies only, so it has no trusts, partnerships or sole traders (by its
  rules, not by choice).
- **Government suppliers** are the most varied: sole traders 16.2% (4.1% of IP filers) and trusts 12.9% (4.1%).
- **Status:** 62.4% of private companies' ABNs are active, 71.8% of public companies' and 34.3% of partnerships'. Of

observations.headline: Firms are a median 13.6 years old on the public record, with a spike where ABNs began
observations.statement: Measured from a firm's earliest public registration, the [[median]] firm is 13.6 years old. The most common start date, 1 November 1999 (5,279 firms), is the day ABNs began, so many of those firms are older than the record shows.

figures.label: years, the median age on the record
firms first seen on 1 November 1999, the ABN's start
of firms dated by their ABN are possibly older than shown

points: The [[mean]] age is 16.32 years, higher than the median because of a long tail of old companies (the oldest was registered in 1817).
By the register that set the date: companies registered with ASIC are a median 14.6 years old, firms dated by GST registration 11.3 and firms dated by their ABN 18.4.
27,403 firms have no date at all.

questions.how: Age lets Stage 2 ask whether younger firms use the IP system differently from established ones.
Stage of business development is one of the conditions Q3 asks about.

prep.what: A firm's age is the years since its earliest public registration (with ASIC, for an ABN, or for GST), up to 22 October 2026, the date the corpus was built.
prep.why: The public registers give only current statuses, so the earliest registration is the best available start date. Fixing the end date stops ages changing with the day the analysis is run.

prep.what: A flag marks firms first seen when ABNs or GST began (1999 to 2000), whose real age may be greater.
prep.why: Their recorded start is the start of the register, not of the business (ADR 0010).

steps: Take each firm's earliest registration date and work out its age in years.
Summarise the ages (median, mean, spread) and find the most common start dates.
Repeat by the register that set each firm's date, and count how many are flagged as possibly older.
assumptions: A firm's earliest public registration is close to when it began. For companies this is usually true; for firms dated by their ABN or GST it may not be, which is why they are flagged.
limits: Age on the record is a lower bound on a business's real age.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses age together with its "possibly older" flag, and looks at firms first seen from 2001 separately.

observations.original:
**U43 (descriptive). Firms are a median 13.6 years old on the record, with a spike at the ABN's start.**
- Median 13.6 years, mean 16.32: a long tail of old companies (the oldest registered in 1817).
- By the register that set the date: ASIC-registered companies a median 14.6 years; firms dated by GST 11.3; by the

observations.headline: A few firms file most of the patents that firms file
observations.statement: Of the 23,971 firms that filed standard patents, the top 1% filed 55.3% of them, while the typical ([[median]]) firm filed just one. Trade marks are less concentrated: the top 1% of filing firms filed 25.9%.

figures.label: of firms' standard patents were filed by the top 1% of filing firms
standard patent filed by the median filing firm
standard patents filed by the busiest single firm

points: **Standard patents.** 23,971 firms filed 183,989; the median firm filed 1 and the [[percentile|90th percentile]] firm 7.
**Trade marks.** 241,576 firms filed 883,165; median 1, 90th percentile 6; the top 1% filed 25.9%.
**Designs.** 12,554 firms filed 74,697, and the top 1% filed 35.8%. Provisional applications: the top 1% of 24,905 firms filed 32.0%. Second-tier patents: the top 1% of 6,077 firms filed 12.2%.
**What firms hold now.** 116,240 firms hold 430,305 rights still in force; the top 1% of them hold 28.7%.
Plotted on [[log-scale|log scales]], the number of firms filing a given number of applications falls in a near-straight line: a [[long-tail]].

questions.how: Use of the system is highly uneven, so national averages would mostly describe a handful of heavy filers. Q2's interest in distribution over averages starts here.
The contrast between the few heavy filers and the many one-off filers is a natural place to look for what distinguishes valuable use of IP.

prep.what: Each application is credited to the business that filed it (the first founding applicant with an ABN).
prep.why: Crediting today's holder would move applications to whoever bought the rights later (ADR 0016).

prep.what: Standard patents, provisional applications, second-tier patents, trade marks and designs are counted apart.
prep.why: They are different rights with different costs and purposes, and a combined count would mostly be trade marks (U4).

prep.what: Only firms with at least one application of a type are counted for that type.
prep.why: The question is how filing is spread among those who file, not how many firms never file.

steps: Start from every standard patent application whose filer has an ABN, credited to that filer.
Count each firm's applications. 23,971 firms filed 183,989 standard patents.
Line the firms up from most to fewest applications.
Take the top 1% of firms in that line and add up their applications.
Divide by all 183,989 applications. The result is 55.3%.
Repeat for each type of right, and for the rights firms hold now.
assumptions: One ABN is one firm. Companies in the same corporate group are counted separately, so concentration by corporate group would be at least as high as shown.
Applications without a filer's ABN (individuals, and some organisations) are outside this count; the shares describe firms with an ABN.
limits: A count of applications says nothing about their value. Heavy filers' patents may be worth more or less than anyone else's.
Firms' IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}), and filers after FY2024 are less often linked to an ABN ({U45}).
observations.next: Stage 2 relates firms' filing to their R&D, contracts, age and type, using medians, logs or ranks rather than averages, because averages would be pulled up by the few heaviest filers.

observations.original:
**U44 (descriptive). Most firms file once or twice; a few file most of the patents.**
- **Standard patents:** 23,971 firms filed 183,989; the median firm filed 1, the 90th percentile 7, the most 3,811.
  The top 1% of filing firms filed 55.3% of them.
- **Trade marks:** 241,576 firms filed 883,165; median 1, 90th percentile 6; the top 1% filed 25.9%.
- **Designs:** 12,554 firms filed 74,697 (top 1%: 35.8%); **provisional applications:** 24,905 firms (32.0%);
  **second-tier patents:** 6,077 firms (12.2%).
- **What firms hold now:** 260,292 firms hold 1,262,125 rights; 116,240 hold 430,305 rights in force (the top 1%
  of those: 28.7%).
- The spread is close to a straight line on log scales (the chart): a long tail, so Stage 2 uses medians, logs or
  ranks for firm counts, never means alone.

observations.headline: Recent filers are less often linked to a business number, so part of an apparent fall in new filers is in the records
observations.statement: Firms filing their first trade mark fell from 11,318 in FY2024 to 7,384 in FY2026. But over the same years the share of Australian organisations' trade marks that carry the filer's [[abn|ABN]] fell from 84.1% to 59.9%. At least part of the fall is in linking applications to businesses, not in filing.

figures.label: Australian organisations' trade marks with the filer's ABN, FY2024 to FY2026
firms filing their first trade mark, FY2024 to FY2026

points: Firms filing their first trade mark rose from 1,186 (FY1990) to 11,318 (FY2024), then fell to 8,741 (FY2025) and 7,384 (FY2026). Firms filing their first patent fell from 1,165 (FY2020) to 685 (FY2026).
The share with a filer's ABN fell for trade marks from 84.1% (FY2024) to 71.4% (FY2025) and 59.9% (FY2026); for designs from 88.4% to 76.3%; for standard patents from 88.7% to 83.9%.
ABNs may be attached to applications late, or collected less often. The data cannot say which.

questions.how: Any trend in who is newly using the system depends on this linking; until it is explained, recent years cannot be compared fairly.
Whether ABNs are collected at filing is something IP Australia controls, so the answer bears on how well it can measure its own reach.

prep.what: Each firm's first application of each type is dated by financial year.
prep.why: The year a firm first files is its entry into the system.

prep.what: The share with a filer's ABN is worked out among Australian organisations only.
prep.why: Individuals usually have no ABN, so including them would mix a change in who files with a change in linking.

steps: Count, for each financial year, the firms whose first trade mark (or patent, or design) was filed that year.
Separately, for Australian organisations' applications in each year, work out the share that carry the filer's ABN.
Compare the two over FY2024 to FY2026. The count of new filers falls while the share linked to an ABN also falls.
assumptions: Australian organisations would normally have an ABN; a falling share with one is read as a change in recording, not a change in who files.
limits: The data cannot separate late linking from less collection, or say how much of the fall in new filers is real.
observations.next: Firm-level filing by year is compared only up to FY2024 until the cause is known. The question has gone to IP Australia (OQ7).

**U45 (descriptive). The latest years' filers are less often linked to an ABN: a lead.**
- Firms filing their first trade mark rose from 1,186 (FY1990) to 11,318 (FY2024), then fell to 8,741 (FY2025) and
  7,384 (FY2026); first patent filers fell from 1,165 (FY2020) to 685 (FY2026).
- But the share of Australian organisations' trade marks with a filer's ABN fell from 84.1% (FY2024) to 71.4%

- **Decision:** firm-level filing by year is compared only to FY2024 until the cause is known (ADR 0016). It is a

observations.headline: R&D claims are spread across many firms; government contract value is concentrated in a few suppliers

observations.headline: Places differ in filing far more than chance would make them
observations.statement: At the national rate (0.99 standard patents a year per 10,000 people), chance alone would put 2.5% of areas above and 2.5% below the 95% limits. Instead 6.7% are above and 68.2% below for standard patents, and 15.0% and 71.4% for trade marks. Pooled into 335 larger areas (SA3s) the pattern holds (15.5% above, 72.5% below).

figures.label: of areas below chance limits for standard patents
expected below by chance alone

points: Most areas file less than the nation, and a few file far more.
Rates are shown for 850 areas for standard patents (82.73% of people) and 2,094 for trade marks (99.46%); 324 of the 335 SA3s would expect 10 or more standard patents.
The highest rate per person is Sydney's centre, 2000 (712.6 trade marks a year per 10,000 people); for standard patents, 2113 (61.8).

questions.how: Real differences between places are the starting point for asking who is underserved; chance cannot explain them away.
Areas far below the national rate are candidates, later, for asking whether something holds them back.

prep.what: A rate is applications a year per 10,000 people over FY2017 to FY2026, shown only where 10 or more would be expected at the national rate.
prep.why: A count of 10 has a 95% chance range of about 5 to 18; below that, an area's rate is mostly chance (ADR 0017).

prep.what: Small areas are pooled into 335 SA3s as a check.
prep.why: If the pattern were small-area noise, pooling would remove it.

steps: Work out the national rate, and each area's expected count at that rate.
Draw the range chance alone would allow around the national rate, for each size of area (a funnel plot).
Count the areas above and below the range.
Repeat for SA3s.
assumptions: Each area's filings would follow a Poisson pattern if only chance were at work.
limits: The funnel shows that areas differ, not why; a single firm can lift an area ({U52}).
observations.next: Stage 2 models area counts with room for this extra spread (negative binomial models), pooled to SA3s, beside the firms behind them.
observations.chapter: 3. Lens: Places (one row per postal area)
observations.original:
**U53 (descriptive). Areas differ far more than chance would make them; rates are shown where they mean something.**
- **The funnels:** at the national rate (18.69 trade marks and 0.99 standard patents a year per 10,000 people), chance
  would put 2.5% of areas above and 2.5% below the 95% limits. Instead 15.0% are above and 71.4% below for trade marks,
  6.7% and 68.2% for standard patents. Most areas file less than the nation, and a few file far more.
- **Pooled into 335 SA3s** the pattern holds (15.5% above, 72.5% below for standard patents), so it is not small-area
  noise. Stage 2 models these counts with room for that spread (negative binomial, not Poisson).
- **Rates shown** (ADR 0017): standard patents per person for 850 areas (82.73% of people), trade marks for 2,094
  (99.46%), designs for 812 (81.16%); per business, 650, 2,048 and 608. 324 of the 335 SA3s would expect 10 or more standard
  patents (99.8% of people).
- **Medians and extremes:** trade marks a median 8.48 a year per 10,000 people (90th percentile 32.61) and 4.35 per
  1,000 businesses. The highest per person is 2000, Sydney's centre (712.6, with 27,940 residents and 70,543
  businesses); per business it is 26.4 there. For standard patents 2113 is highest (61.8 per 10,000 people).

observations.headline: Half of R&D claimants have never filed for IP, and claimants are rarer outside the cities
observations.statement: Of 17,627 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants placed in a postal area, 50.7% have never filed IP as a founding applicant. There are 5.6 claimants per 1,000 businesses in major cities, 2.4 in inner regional, 1.8 in outer regional, 1.3 in remote and 0.6 in very remote areas.

IP-filing firms: 49.7 per 1,000 businesses in the cities, against 19.0 to 29.3 elsewhere.
These are counts by registered address, not necessarily where the R&D is done.

questions.how: Firms doing R&D that never use the IP system ('missing filers') are an obvious group to ask about later, for barriers IP Australia could ease.
R&D without IP is one of the alternatives to registration Q3 asks about.

prep.what: Firms are placed by their business register postcode; "never filed" means never a founding applicant with this ABN.
prep.why: Filing is credited to the business that filed (ADR 0016).

steps: Count active claimants and IP-filing firms in each postal area.
Count claimants who never filed IP.
Group by remoteness and divide by businesses.
assumptions: A claimant with no IP under its own ABN has not filed; filings under a related company's ABN are missed.
limits: A lower bound on IP use: firms' IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}).
observations.next: Stage 2 studies 'missing filers' by place and industry.

observations.headline: Values split from larger areas track direct counts; CABEE counts a quarter fewer businesses than the business register
observations.statement: Data by Region's 2021 population, split from larger areas, is within 10% of the direct count for 99.34% of postal areas of 1,000 people or more. CABEE's June 2025 business count is 0.742 of the register's active GST businesses, but ranks areas almost alike (Spearman 0.988): they count different things.

CABEE's count as a share of the register's

points: The Census's count (25,369,823) is the geography's count (25,365,506) to within 0.02%, the gap being the ABS's privacy adjustment.
CABEE counts businesses actively trading; the register counts registrations. So a CABEE count is never compared with a register count.

questions.how: Confirms the method for placing other data in postal areas, and which business count to use.

prep.what: The same quantity is taken from two routes and compared, area by area.
prep.why: Agreement shows the splitting method works; disagreement shows the measures differ.

steps: For each area, compare the Census and split population with the geography's count.

observations.statement: Before records were computerised, the register holds only rights still alive then. Only 2.0% of trade marks filed in early 1981 were never registered, against 52.0% from the first quarter of 1983. So those years count survivors, not filings, and fifteen series now start later. The rise of the patent term from 16 to 20 years (1 July 1995) was missing from the policy list and has been added.

points: **Designs:** 0.4% and 0.7% never registered in the second half of 1985, then 26.3% in the first quarter of 1986.
**Batches.** Patent cessations were dated in batches to April 1995: 29.8% of the 104 months from September 1986 hold none.
**Partial records.** Grants are recorded only for patents filed from 1979: 1.0% to 1.9% of standard patents filed in 1976 to 1978 have a grant date, against 68.5% of those filed in 1979.
**Real, not an artefact:** patent expiries all but stop from July 1995 and resume in July 1999, because every patent then in force gained four more years.

For event series, find months with no events followed by backlogs: signs of batch dating.
Set each series' start after these, and check the patent expiry series against the 1995 Act.

**U23 (descriptive). Fifteen series started too early, and one policy change was missing (ADR 0014).**
- **Survivors.** By quarter of filing, 2.0% of trade marks filed in early 1981 were never registered, 22.6% in the
  third quarter of 1982 and 52.0% from the first quarter of 1983 (51.0% at the end of 1988). Of designs, 0.4% and 0.7%
  in the second half of 1985, then 26.3% in the first quarter of 1986. Provisional applications run at 251 to 355 a
  quarter in the quarters shown before mid-1985, and 1,372 in the last quarter of 1985. A register that keeps only what survived records almost no
  failures, so the earlier months count survivors, not filings: 44,207 trade marks from Australian applicants and
  75,506 from overseas ones over the 921 months from April 1906 (3.2% and 8.4% of each series).
- **Batches.** Patent cessations were dated in batches to April 1995: 29.8% of the 104 months from September 1986 hold
  none, and others hold several months' worth (46,671 cessations, 11% of the series). Expiries to December 1994 hold
  29.4% of their series. Both are dated weekly or daily since (the chart).
- **Partial records.** IP RAPID records grants only for patents filed from 1979: 1.0% to 1.9% of standard patents
  filed in 1976 to 1978 have a grant date, against 68.5% of those filed in 1979. So the 16,557 grants before 1985 are
  some of the grants made (2.5% of the series).
- **What remains real.** Patent expiries all but stop from July 1995 and resume in July 1999 (the chart; measured in
  5.4). Australia raised the standard patent term from 16 to 20 years on 1 July 1995, for every patent still
  in force, so patents filed from July 1979 expired four years later than they would have. The policy register now
  holds this change, checked against the Act (the Patents (World Trade Organization Amendments) Act 1994), and its
  note on the Patents Act 1990, which said the 1990 Act brought in 20-year patents, is corrected: the 1990 Act's term
  was 16 years.

steps: Add up each event series by calendar year.
Find each series' peak year.

- **Patent grants** peaked in 2016 (25,687), three years after the rush to file before Raising the Bar (5.4), and

- **Trade mark registrations** rose from 19,578 (1996) to 70,634 (2021, the peak) and 70,616 (2025).
- **Lapses** (applications that ended): patents peaked in 2010 (13,945) and were 12,294 in 2025; trade marks peaked
  in 2017 (19,767).
- **Cessations** (registered rights let go) rose for trade marks from 7,240 (1996) to 35,484 (2025, the peak), and for
  patents from 8,202 to 18,919 (2021, the peak) and 15,244 (2025). Design cessations were 6,218 to 6,612 in each year
  shown since 2016.
- **Expiries** of patents rose from 30 (1996) and 861 (2000) to 4,019 (2025), as patents filed under the 20-year term

- **Ownership transfers:** trade mark assignments rose from 9,389 (1996) to 18,370 (2019, the peak); patent

observations.headline: Policy changes leave clear marks, two rushes, four steps and two pauses, while several leave none
observations.statement: Before Raising the Bar (April 2013), Australians filed 1,018 standard patents in a month, 4.39 times their average month in the year before. Before the innovation patent closed (August 2021), 2,789 second-tier applications came in one month (4.31 times), then 95.9% fewer. Patent expiries fell 98.4% when the term rose to 20 years.

second-tier applications after the innovation patent closed
patent expiries after the term rose to 20 years

points: **Rushes:** Raising the Bar (Australians 4.39 times, overseas 2.66 times their usual month) and the innovation patent's closure. Anticipation also shows after each was enacted.

**Steps:** patent expiries (the 20-year term), extensions of term (the 1999 scheme, from 0.08 to 11.17 a month), second-tier applications when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent (+71.5%), and designs under the Designs Act 2003 (overseas applications +34.1%).
**Pauses when an Act began:** no trade mark registrations in January 1996 (Trade Marks Act 1995) and 113 patent grants in June 1991 (Patents Act 1990), against about 1,025 a month.

questions.how: These dated changes are the raw material for natural experiments, the designs that can estimate what a policy actually changed.
Shows which levers have moved behaviour visibly in the past, and which have not.

prep.what: Each of the 17 policy changes is placed in the month it took effect (or, for two, was enacted), checked against the Federal Register of Legislation.
prep.why: A wrong date would put the change in the wrong place (ADR 0011, 0014).

prep.what: Each change is paired with the series it targets.
prep.why: A change to trade mark law should show in trade mark series, not patents.

steps: For each change, take its target series for 24 months either side.
Compare the change's month and the 12 months after with the average month of the 12 before.
Class each response as a rush, a step, a pause or nothing visible.
assumptions: The change caused what is seen around it. Stage 1 only describes timing; trends, seasons and other events could also be at work.
limits: Fee changes, IP Australia's most direct lever, are not yet in the data (OQ2).
observations.next: Stage 2 measures each candidate against trends and seasons, with placebo dates.
observations.section: 5.4 The 17 policy changes, one at a time
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**U28 (descriptive). Four kinds of response, and changes with none visible.** All compare the average month in the
12 months after a change's month with the 12 months before; trends and seasons are not allowed for.
- **Rushes to file before a change.** Raising the Bar (April 2013): 1,018 standard patent applications from
  Australians (4.39 times their average month in the year before) and 5,407 from overseas (2.66 times); in the year
  after, 34.0% and 7.6% fewer a month. The innovation patent's closure (August 2021): 2,789 applications (4.31 times),
  then 95.9% fewer (26.25 a month). Anticipation shows after each enactment: second-tier applications rose 176.4% in
  the year after the phase-out was enacted, and Australian standard patents 45.3% in the year after Raising the Bar
  was.
- **Steps.** Patent expiries fell 98.4% (289.5 to 4.67 a month) when the term rose to 20 years. Extensions of term
  went from 0.08 a month to 11.17 under the 1999 regime (60 in December 1999, the chart). Second-tier applications
  rose 71.5% (50.58 to 86.75 a month) when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent. Under the Designs Act
  2003, design applications from overseas rose 34.1% and registrations 24.5%; Australians' applications 6.5%.
- **Pauses at commencement.** The Trade Marks Act 1995: no trade mark registrations in January 1996, 4,021 in March
  (5.5), and Australians' applications at 0.49 times their usual month in January 1996; assignments published rose
  79.3%. The Patents Act 1990: 113 patent grants in June 1991, against about 1,025 a month (5.5).
- **None visible:** Australia joining the PCT (March 1980; entries through it come about 30 months after filing
  abroad); the plain packaging of tobacco (Australian trade marks −3.9%, overseas +5.2%, and no series counts tobacco
  marks); the Productivity Commission responses of 2018 and 2019 (trade mark oppositions +3.1%); the designs grace
  period (2022: Australians −16.5%, overseas +0.2%). Overseas trade marks fell 16.4% in the year after Australia
  joined the Madrid Protocol (July 2001), but the chart shows them falling from early 2000. Plant breeder's rights
  applications rose 22% after the 1994 Act, on 21 to 25 a month: too few to read.
- **Decision:** Stage 2's candidates are the two rushes, the four steps and the two pauses, each with placebo dates.
  The register still lacks fee changes (R3), the other lever IP Australia holds.

observations.headline: Forty-two months still stand out after the repairs; each is explained and kept
observations.statement: After the repairs, 42 months in 12 series are at least three times, or under a third of, the months around them. They are rushes, the register's start-up in 1904, pauses and backlogs when new Acts began, and one transfer of many patents at once (1,603 patent assignments in July 2015).

figures.label: unusual months, all explained
patent assignments in July 2015, one large transfer

points: **Pauses and backlogs:** patent grants in June 1991 (113); trade mark registrations in January and March 1996 (0, then 4,021); patent cessations in February 2020 (7).
**The register's first months:** applications could be lodged from February 1904, before the Patents Act 1903 took effect on 1 June 1904.
**Design lapses** fall to 0 to 16 in April in six of the seven years from 1996 to 2002 ({U39}).
**The July 2015 transfer:** the patents assigned on 2 July 2015 are now held mostly in Finland (198) and the United States (170).
**Decision.** No more months are removed; pauses are pooled with their backlogs, rushes are studied.

questions.how: Unusual months must be explained before any month can be read as a policy effect.

prep.what: Each month is compared with the median of the two years around it, in series running at 50 or more a month.
prep.why: A two-year median is not pulled about by one odd month.

steps: For each series, work out the median of the 25 months centred on each month.
Flag months at least three times or under a third of it.
Look up what happened in each flagged month.
assumptions: A month three times its neighbours is unusual enough to need explaining.
limits: Smaller oddities are not flagged.
observations.next: Stage 2 pools pauses with their backlogs, or uses 12-month totals.

observations.original:
**U29 (descriptive). What still stands out, and what it is.** The table lists 42 months in 12 series.
- **Rushes, kept:** April 2013 (Australian standard patents, 5.36 times the median of the two years around it) and
  August 2021 (second-tier patents, 6 times). They are the policy responses of U28.
- **The register's first months:** standard patents of unknown origin run at 0 to 35 a month from January to May 1904
  and 394 in June 1904. Applications could be lodged from February 1904, before the Patents Act 1903 took effect on
  1 June 1904, so the months before June are a start-up, best left out of any comparison.
- **Pauses and their backlogs, kept:** patent grants in June 1991 (113, after the Patents Act 1990 commenced) and in
  October and November 1998 (248, then 3,373); trade mark registrations in January and March 1996 (0, then 4,021, the
  Trade Marks Act 1995); patent cessations in December 2006 (82) and February 2020 (7). February 2020 is also the
  month the innovation patent's phase-out was enacted, but the pause is in cessations of every kind of patent, so
  nothing in the data links the two.
- **Single low months in steady series:** trade mark registrations in January 1987 (151) and September 1991 (339),
  design registrations in January 1992 (77), trade mark lapses in October 1986, August 1987 and April 1996 (122, 94
  and 243), and patent assignments in February 1992, August 1998, January 2000 and March 2026 (42 to 75); patent
  assignments were also high in June 1994 (347).
- **A recurring low:** design lapses fall to 0 to 16 in April in six of the seven years from 1996 to 2002, and to 0 in
  October 2002, in a series of 59 to 76 a month. A lead, too small to matter elsewhere.
- **The origin field, not the count:** trade marks of unknown origin fall to 14 to 40 a month from November 1983 to
  May 1984 (and 87 in July 1985), against about 240. Australian and overseas trade marks are not flagged in those
  months, so what changed is the origin recorded.
- **An effect of the method:** patent expiries in February 1995 (240, 3.22 times) stand out only because the two years
  around them include the near-empty months after July 1995 (U23).
- **A transfer of many patents at once:** patent assignments in July 2015 (1,603, 4.2 times the median), published
  over the month's five weekly issues (395, 646, 325, 163 and 73); the patents assigned on 2 July 2015 are now held
  mostly in Finland (198) and the United States (170). One transfer of a portfolio fits this; the data do not name it.
- **Decision:** no further months are removed. Stage 2 pools each pause with its backlog (for example, patent
  cessations in February and March 2020) or uses 12-month totals; rushes are studied, not removed; the months before
  June 1904 are left out.

observations.statement: The price index has 312 quarters, from the September quarter 1948 to the June quarter 2026, with none missing. Prices rose about 40-fold, from 2.59 to 102.31. Price rises have run at a median 2.3% a year from 1990 to 2019 and 3.6% from 2020 to 2026.

observations.original:
**U30 (descriptive). The CPI is complete, quarterly, from 1948.**
- 312 quarters, from the September quarter 1948 to the June quarter 2026, with none missing.
- Its base is the month of September 2025 (= 100), as the ABS labels it. A quarter is the average of its three months
  (July to September 2025: 99.63, 99.55 and 100.0), so the September quarter 2025 is 99.73.
- Prices rose about 40-fold: from 2.59 (September quarter 1948) to 102.31 (June quarter 2026).
- The median change over four quarters was 3.0% from 1949 to 1969 (highest 25.6%, to the December quarter 1951), 8.7%
  from 1970 to 1989 (17.5%, March quarter 1975), 2.3% from 1990 to 2019 and 3.6% from 2020 to 2026 (7.9%, December
  quarter 2022). Prices fell in 13 quarters.
- **Decision:** money series are deflated with this quarterly index, and shown as recorded beside it, with the base
  stated. `abs_prices` also holds the monthly CPI from April 2024 (29 months); it is not attached, as one series
  must serve the whole span.
